o: We must split nums into two halves of equal size, each containing distinct elements. Distinctness within a part means any value can appear at most once per part, hence at most twice overall — once in nums1 and once in nums2. In Example 1 frequencies are 1,1,2,2,1,1 (all ≤ 2), so we can deal the duplicated values one-to-each-part and distribute singles to balance sizes: true. In Example 2 the value 1 appears four times, forcing a duplicate inside some part: false. So the entire problem collapses to one frequency check.
k: A value may appear at most once in each part, so the split is possible iff every value occurs at most twice.
Equal part sizes are then automatic: put one copy of each doubled value in each part and split the singleton values arbitrarily between the two parts.

a.i: Count occurrences of each value. If any count exceeds 2, some part must contain a repeated value, which is forbidden. Otherwise a valid balanced split always exists, so we just return whether the maximum frequency is ≤ 2.
s: Build a frequency map of nums.
If any frequency is greater than 2, return false.
Otherwise return true (sizes balance out because n is even).
a.t: O(n) — one pass to count, one pass over distinct values.

w: The key interview moment is proving sufficiency: with all frequencies ≤ 2, place one copy of every twice-occurring value into each part, then hand out singleton values one-by-one alternating between parts; since the total count is even, both parts end at size n/2. Pitfall: confusing this with 'each part needs distinct values relative to the other part' — the parts may share values (Example 1 shares 1 and 2). A natural follow-up asks to actually output a valid split, which the alternating assignment constructs in O(n).
